grader: Graded 2026-09-24 by the agent under Omar Saleem's delegation ("you should be able to do that from the guide"); rule set below; final review Dr. Hannah-Shmouni
gradingRule: Grade = certainty the source gives for the specific clinical statement the lesson makes, on the guides' A–D scale. A: consistent large RCTs or approval-grade evidence. B: at least one well-designed, adequately powered RCT or an independent, quality-stratified meta-analysis (either direction). C: small or sponsor-funded RCTs without independent replication, or pooled trials dominated by them. D: animal, in-vitro, mechanistic, case series, manufacturer dossiers. 'context' = history, reviews used for framing, trial registrations without results, analytical or regulatory records (regulatory records are primary for status statements, not graded for efficacy). Where the two guides disagree, the lesson states both and the claim takes the grade the primary evidence supports. Observational studies (added 2026-09-24, GRADE starting point, for the final reviewer to confirm): adequately sized cohort, case-control or cross-sectional studies grade C for the association they measured; small or single-centre ones grade D; any causal claim drawn from observational data grades D. Meta-analyses of observational studies grade at most B, and only for association. Guidelines and consensus statements are 'context', cited for what they recommend, not graded as evidence.

claims.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and cGMP only if the bulk substance meets a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list — and is made by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis. Quality is defined by reference to those standards and the certificate, not by a numerical purity threshold in the statute's text.

503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, must meet cGMP, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, report adverse events and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions; their products are exempt from approval and adequate-directions requirements, so they remain unapproved.
As of 22 September 2026 the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) holds six substances, none a peptide, unchanged since 2019; listing carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.

claims.text: Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, not listing. claims.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot — mass spectrometry for identity (observed against expected mass), HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results. It cannot establish that the vial in hand is that lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject; lot-less, chromatogram-less, stale (over 12 months) and endotoxin-less certificates are warning signs.

claims.text: There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram: FDA's guidance says the limit is calculated with the USP method from the product's dosage regimen and strength, and some routes (intrathecal, ophthalmic) differ.

FDA's July 2026 briefing on BPC-157 found the nominators' certificates described a different form (the acetate) from the one nominated, that publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits, and that the nominator's certificate mentioned no endotoxin test.

Paperwork and contents can diverge: three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label, 29–39% more peptide than labelled and endotoxin in every vial; a seized injection vial held an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Neither study concerns skin peptides.

claims.text: 'Not for use in humans' research labelling (21 CFR 312.160) permits shipment only for laboratory or in-vitro research, and FDA reads intended use objectively from claims, advertising and the circumstances of distribution (21 CFR 201.128); a research-use-only product therefore has no clinical route, and a certificate does not create one.

claims.text: In the US the regime follows intended use and route: appearance claims make a cosmetic (no premarket approval), while a claim to affect structure or function — such as 'regenerate cells' — makes a drug, and 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning; dietary supplements are not approved before sale, their makers being responsible for safety and labelling.

authorFindings: Peptide Pocket Guide, 'The FDA's regulatory line' table (peptide fundamentals) — the rows '41–99 alpha amino acids, chemically synthesized: still regulated as a drug' and '≥100: always a protein regardless of synthesis route' reflect FDA's 2018 proposal. The Further Consolidated Appropriations Act 2020 removed the 'chemically synthesized polypeptide' exception, and FDA's final rule (85 FR 10057, effective 23 March 2020) defines any alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids as a protein; FDA did not finalize the 41–99 interpretation. Tesamorelin (44 residues, which the guide lists among polypeptides) was itself deemed a biologics licence on 23 March 2020.

Peptide Pocket Guide — 'biologics … are largely ineligible for 503A pharmacy compounding' and, in the Lilly v. FDA case study, '503A compounding of biologics operates under different authority': FDA's March 2020 notice to compounders states that biological products subject to licensure under PHS Act 351 (including deemed BLAs such as hyaluronidase and hCG) are not eligible for the 503A or 503B exemptions. Suggest stating it that plainly.

Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology ch. 3 ref 4 and ch. 20 ref 3 give the PCAC docket as 'FDA-2026-N-2979'; the Federal Register notice (91 FR 20465, doc 2026-07361) is Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895, as the Peptide Pocket Guide prints.

Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology ch. 15 table, ch. 20 regulatory pearl and the drug-safety table place BPC-157, TB-500, CJC-1295, ipamorelin and epitalon in '503A Category 2'. FDA's safety-risks page (content current 22 April 2026) lists them in the table of withdrawn nominations, in no category (ipamorelin remains in 503B Category 2), and 503A Category 2 holds six substances as of 14 May 2026. The Peptide Pocket Guide (August build) is current on this point.

Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology ch. 3 decision frame and the 'peptide decision framework' algorithm reduce 503A eligibility to 'on the current positive bulks list'. The statute's routes are hierarchical — USP/NF monograph, then component of an approved drug, then the bulks list — with Category 1 enforcement discretion (e.g., non-injectable GHK-Cu) a separate interim posture. The course teaches the statutory order.

Peptide Pocket Guide, 'For research-use-only peptides' (peptide fundamentals) — the steps offered 'if the product is being used outside its labelled purpose' (independent MS and HPLC, an endotoxin test before injectable use, dose-by-dose documentation) read as harm-reduction instructions for human use of products labelled 'Not for use in humans' (21 CFR 312.160), and sit awkwardly beside the guide's own 'the RUO disclaimer provides no legal protection'. The course omits them; suggest reframing as what a clinician records when a patient discloses use.

Peptide Pocket Guide — the two GRADE definition pages disagree: 'How strong is the evidence?' defines D as animal, in-vitro or mechanistic reasoning only and C as including conflicting results; 'Where the GRADE ratings come from' adds 'industry-driven claims' to D. Suggest one definition, mapped explicitly to GRADE's four certainty levels and its five rating-down domains.
Peptide Pocket Guide, jurisdictional snapshot — 'most malpractice policies exclude unapproved-drug claims' carries no citation and could not be verified; the course does not use it.

FDA's July 2026 BPC-157 briefing (fda.gov/media/193343) is primary evidence both guides could cite in their certificate-of-analysis sections: the nominators' certificates were for BPC-157 acetate while the nomination was for the free base, publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits, and the nominator's certificate reported no endotoxin test. The same document cites a single small exploratory trial in ulcerative colitis reported only as a meeting abstract.

Not in either guide, worth adding — the Core GRADE series (BMJ 2025) as the current GRADE reference; the Cochrane review of industry sponsorship and research outcome (Lundh 2017); FDA's endotoxin Q&A guidance (Edition 2, March 2026) for the dose-and-route basis of endotoxin limits; FDA's 'Is It a Cosmetic, a Drug, or Both?' page, whose drug-claim examples include 'regenerate cells'; and Popławska 2019 (an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue found in a seized vial by high-resolution MS).
